# Unremarkable

Canonical page: https://unremarkable.me/

> **Design fiction.** Unremarkable is written as if it were a business. It isn't taking work yet. What that means: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

Websites for the people who use them, and the agents they send.

People come to your website to do something: find an answer, choose a service, book a place. Increasingly, they send an agent to do it for them. We design, build and look after websites for both.

We start with your organisation and what people come to you to achieve. Then we build a distinctive site that makes your offer clear and helps them get things done, however they arrive. Every design is tested by ear, by someone who uses a screen reader every day.

Start a website

- **AAA** contrast on every word, in light and dark
- **0** cookies, so no cookie banner
- **0** lines of JavaScript
- **By ear** every kind of page heard with a screen reader before it goes live

## Our work

These are our own sites: working publications where we develop and use the approach we offer here. We depend on them ourselves, and what we build gets used on them first.

1. [**blind-ant.com**](https://blind-ant.com/): ![A white card describing the Blind Ant logo in words.](https://unremarkable.me/pictures/work-blind-ant.webp) A making practice that publishes often: design fiction, stories, games and apps. Its pieces are published from an in-tray, twice a day, by its own agent, the one Cloud Dancer is modelled on, and the worked example is one of its jobs.
2. [**carrados.com**](https://carrados.com/): ![The Carrados logo, a letter C with an eye inside it, on cream.](https://unremarkable.me/pictures/work-carrados.webp) Writing about AI and blindness that has to be accountable for its evidence: the frameworks, the Papers and The Blind AI, with a desk and an address of its own for each of its writers.
3. [**charli-jo.com**](https://charli-jo.com/): ![Dark green headings on cream, starting with Charli-Jo Tyrer.](https://unremarkable.me/pictures/work-charli-jo.webp) A practice in accessible service design for people and the agents they send. Its principle and method began as Word documents and are now kept as the pages themselves.
4. [**charli.info**](https://charli.info/): ![Deep purple headings on white, starting with The CharliVerse.](https://unremarkable.me/pictures/work-charli.webp) The front door of the CharliVerse, a shared fictional world, and CharliPedia, its memory: an encyclopaedia people and agents can read, with a connector that lets compatible AI tools look things up directly.
5. [**Zero Information Casualty**](https://zeroinformationcasualty.org/): ![The title, Zero Information Casualty v1.7, in dark green.](https://unremarkable.me/pictures/work-zeroinformationcasualty.webp) The web standard every one of these sites is built to, published on a site built to it.

## The rule

Unremarkable has one rule, and it overrides every other: **it never is.**

Every site we make has to impress everyone who meets it, whether they see it, hear it through a screen reader, feel it in braille or send an agent to fetch it for them. A site that dazzles the eye and stumbles in a screen reader isn't impressive. It's half finished.

## How we build

- **Built for people who hear the web.** Not run through a checker and declared done. Every kind of page in your design is listened to before it goes live, every change is made within that design, and the design is heard again every month.
- **Built for the agents people send.** Every page has a Markdown version, and every site has an llms.txt, so an AI agent sent by a person gets what that person would, from the menu to the footer.
- **Built to a standard.** [Zero Information Casualty v1.7](https://zeroinformationcasualty.org/) means nothing published is lost on its way to any reader.
- **No plugins to patch.** Plain pages served fast from the edge on Cloudflare: no plugins to update, no database to break into, and not a line of JavaScript needed to read a word.
- **Yours, all of it.** Your site, code, domain and hosting account belong to you. You pay the running costs directly, and we work inside your accounts.
- **Leave with everything.** If you stop, your site stays live, and you keep everything another developer, or an agent you trust, needs to carry on.

## Intention-based publishing

Looking after your site is just as straightforward. Send us what you want changed: an email, a document, a flyer or some photographs. We prepare the change on a private copy of your site. Open it on your own device, see how it works, and tell us to publish it or change it again. No editor to learn.

- ![A smiling cloud with arms and legs, kicking up one foot as it dances.](https://unremarkable.me/pictures/cloud-dancer.svg) **Cloud Dancer** is our publishing agent. It prepares the changes you ask for.
- ![A round, smiling character holding a spanner, with a sparkle beside it.](https://unremarkable.me/pictures/phix.svg) **Phix** (said "fix") is our fixing agent. It looks into the problems your visitors report.

Both are built on Claude. We run the service and stand behind the work.

[See a real publishing job](https://unremarkable.me/worked-example/)

[How it works](https://unremarkable.me/how-it-works/)

## This site is Unremarkable

When you find those four words at the foot of a page, the site is ours. Hold it to the rule. Below them is a link, "Fix something on this page". Use it, and Phix will look into it, and we will put it right.

## Start here

We believe the web is moving from competing for attention towards fulfilling intentions. Unremarkable helps you serve the people who visit and the agents they send.

Tell us what people come to you to do. That is where we start.

[Start a website](https://unremarkable.me/start/)

[See the prices](https://unremarkable.me/prices/)

# How it works

Canonical page: https://unremarkable.me/how-it-works/

> **Design fiction.** Unremarkable is written as if it were a business. It isn't taking work yet. What that means: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

You tell us what people come to you to do. We build the website that lets them do it.

## From first conversation to live

1. **A conversation.** What you offer, who comes to you and what they are trying to get done: book a place, find an answer, choose a service. That understanding shapes everything else.
2. **Your accounts, in your name.** We help you open a Cloudflare account for hosting and a GitHub organisation for the code, and register the domain to you. You add us as a member of each. For email and files we recommend Google Workspace and set it up for you, including the records that keep your email out of spam. If you already use Microsoft 365, that works too.
3. **Design and build.** A design made for you, not a theme. You see each version on a private preview address, and you can listen to it as well as look at it.
4. **Tested by ear.** Before it goes live, every kind of page in the design is tested with a screen reader by someone who uses one every day, and the site gets an accessibility statement that says what was checked and when.
5. **Live, and handed over.** The site goes live with a handover note: how it is published, where reports go, how to remove us as a member, and instructions another developer or an AI agent could follow to look after it without us.

## Intention-based publishing

Tell us what you want. We prepare it on a private copy of your site. You decide what goes live.

There is no editor and no content management system to learn. Your website is changed the way you would ask a person to change it.

1. **Say what you want.** Put it in your in-tray: a shared folder in your own Google Drive, or one email address. Write it in your own words, or drop in what you already have, a flyer, a document, the photos from the event: the opening hours are wrong, add the June event, put this on the services page.
2. **See it on your own site.** We make the change on a private copy of your site and send you a link to it. Open it on your own phone or computer, with your own screen reader or magnifier if you use one: the way your visitors will meet it, not a preview in somebody else's tool.
3. **Publish, or change it again.** If it's right, publish it, and it's live. If it isn't, say what's still wrong, and it goes round again. Nothing reaches your visitors until you say so.

Cloud Dancer, our publishing agent, built on Claude, turns what you send into a proposed change. We build and run that process, handle anything that goes wrong, and stand behind every change it makes.

Every change is made within the design you agreed, and that design has already been heard. Automated checks run on every change, and the receipt sets out anything Cloud Dancer wrote itself, such as a picture's description, so you can check it. A new kind of page is heard before it goes live, and the whole design is heard again every month.

No editor also means nothing for a screen reader to stumble over. If you can write an email, you can run your website.

Things that change often, such as events, news and opening times, can live in a Google Sheet that your site reads when it is published. You edit something you already know how to use.

[A real job, start to finish](https://unremarkable.me/worked-example/)

Fixing works the same way. Visitors get their own link, "Fix something on this page", for anything that stops them, whether they read by eye, by screen reader, by braille or by agent. The fix is made on a private copy and tested the way the problem was described, and when it's right, you publish it. Nobody gives an email address: whoever reported it gets a link to their report's own page, which tells them when the fix is live and asks whether it works for them now. If it doesn't, it goes round again. Every report is read first by Phix (said "fix"), our fixing agent, built on Claude. It finds the problem, makes the fix on a private copy and sends it to you. You publish it or send it back with your reasons. Nothing Phix makes goes live without you, and every fix leaves a test behind, so the same problem can't quietly come back.

### A fix, start to finish

1. **Reported** A visitor uses "Fix something on this page" and says what went wrong.
2. **Fixed** Phix finds the cause and fixes it on a private copy of your site.
3. **Checked** You try the fix, then publish it, or send it back with your reasons.
4. **Asked** The visitor's own page tells them it's live, and asks whether it works for them now.
5. **Works for me** If it doesn't, it goes round again.

[How the loop was designed: Works For Me, on blind-ant.com](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/works-for-me/)

## You own everything

The site, its source code, the hosting account and the domain are all yours, and you pay the running costs directly. We work inside your accounts as a member. Your pages are plain HTML and a short build script in your own repository, so any developer, or any agent you send, can pick them up. The forms run on Cloudflare, and would need adapting to move them anywhere else.

[Questions about your accounts and what they cost](https://unremarkable.me/questions/)

## No plugins to patch

Most of the cost of a website built on a platform comes after launch: plugin updates, security patches and cleaning up after break-ins. Our sites are plain pages served from the edge, with no plugins and no database behind them, so there are no plugins to patch and very little that can break. What little code there is, the build script and the forms, we keep up to date as part of looking after your site.

## What we don't build

Online shops. Shopify and WooCommerce are good at them. We build sites for organisations whose visitors come to find out, choose, book and ask: charities, practices, venues, clubs and small firms.

# Prices

Canonical page: https://unremarkable.me/prices/

> **Design fiction.** Unremarkable is written as if it were a business. It isn't taking work yet. What that means: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

One price to build your site, and one monthly price to look after it.

## The build

- **Price:** from £3,500, paid in two halves: one when we start and one when the site goes live
- **Includes:** the conversation, the design, the build, setting up your accounts and email records, testing with a screen reader, the accessibility statement and the handover note
- **Takes:** four to six weeks for most sites

The price depends on how many kinds of page your site needs, not how many pages it has. A site with a hundred events costs no more than a site with ten.

## Looking after it

- **Price:** £75 a month, cancel with a month's notice
- **Includes:** changes to your content and pages within the agreed design, sent to your in-tray; every visitor report from "Fix something on this page"; keeping the build script, forms and agent files up to date; and the whole design heard again by ear each month
- **Turnaround:** content changes made within two working days, and work started within one working day on anything that stops a visitor
- **Not included:** new features, such as a booking system, and redesigns, which are priced before any work starts

Most fixes are made the same day. Some causes sit outside the site, with a browser, a screen reader or a provider, and then we tell you what we found and what we are doing about it.

## If you leave

You own the website. The monthly price pays for the service that changes and looks after it. When you stop, you choose how your site carries on.

### Take your own agent

- **Price:** £750, once
- **Includes:** your own copy of Cloud Dancer, our publishing agent, set up in your own Claude account and named by you; and a training session for whoever will use it

You keep asking for changes the way you always have, in your in-tray, and you still see each change on a private copy before you say publish. Your site keeps growing without us.

- You pay Anthropic for Claude directly. Charities may get it at a discount through Claude for Nonprofits.
- Visitor reports from "Fix something on this page" come to you by email, for your agent or a person to act on.
- From then on the agent is yours. It no longer gets our improvements, and we no longer stand behind the changes it makes.

### Keep it as it is

- Your site stays live. It is in your accounts, and it doesn't need us to stay up.
- We stop watching your in-tray, and changes stop being made for you.
- You keep the complete repository, with written instructions that another developer, or an AI agent you trust, can follow to change and publish it.
- We take our "Fix something on this page" link off your pages, or hand its reports over to whoever looks after the site next.
- We remove ourselves as members of your accounts, and tell you when it's done.

## Running costs, paid by you

- **Domain:** usually £10 to £40 a year, depending on the ending
- **Hosting:** nothing for most sites on Cloudflare's free plan, because visits to plain pages aren't charged; if your forms get very busy, Cloudflare's paid plan is from US$5 a month, plus usage above what it includes; we watch your usage and tell you when we recommend it
- **Email and files:** Google Workspace is charged per person per month, and is free for eligible charities through Google for Nonprofits

You pay these to the providers directly. We never mark them up, because we never hold them.

[Questions about your accounts and what they cost](https://unremarkable.me/questions/)

## Charities

Registered charities get 20% off the build.

# Who's Unremarkable

Canonical page: https://unremarkable.me/about/

> **Design fiction.** Unremarkable is written as if it were a business. It isn't taking work yet. What that means: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

![Charli, smiling, in a sunny coffee shop, in a pink shirt and pink trainers.](https://unremarkable.me/pictures/charli-full.webp) Charli. Photo tidied up with AI.

I'm [Charli-Jo Tyrer](https://charli-jo.com/), Charli for short. I build Unremarkable's websites, and I use a screen reader every day.

That's why every page I build is heard before it goes live. I listen to it the way many of the people who use it will: reading from top to bottom, moving by headings, tabbing through the links. Most websites are made by eye and checked for accessibility at the end, if at all. Mine start with the ear.

## How I work

I decide, and agents build. Claude writes the code. Cloud Dancer, our publishing agent, makes the changes you ask for, and Phix (said "fix"), our fixing agent, looks into the problems your visitors report. Both work on a private copy of your site, and nothing goes live until you say so.

I stand behind every change they make. If something goes wrong, it's mine to put right.

Charli

## What I've built

Every site listed under [Our work](https://unremarkable.me/#our-work) is mine, and this one too. Each ends with "Fix something on this page", and I read what comes back.

# Questions

Canonical page: https://unremarkable.me/questions/

> **Design fiction.** Unremarkable is written as if it were a business. It isn't taking work yet. What that means: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

Where your website lives, what keeps it running, and what that costs you.

## Where your website lives

### Where is my website?

In three places, all in your name. Its files are in your own GitHub organisation. It is live on Cloudflare, in your own account. And its address, the domain, is registered to you.

We work inside those accounts as a member, and you can remove us whenever you like. That is the whole of our hold on your website.

### What does GitHub do?

GitHub keeps your website's files: every page, every picture, and the short build script that turns them into a website. They sit in a repository, a folder that remembers every change ever made, who made it and why, so any earlier version can be brought back.

You never need to open it. You ask for changes in your in-tray, and we make them. GitHub is what lets you take the whole website with you, and lets any developer or agent you choose carry on where we left off.

### What does Cloudflare do?

Cloudflare puts your website in front of visitors, from a network that spans the world, so a page opens quickly wherever someone is. There is no server of yours to update, patch or keep running. That is Cloudflare's job.

Your forms run on Cloudflare as small programs called Workers. Your domain's settings live there too, in the same account.

### How does a change go live?

Every change waits on a private copy of your site first, where you try it. When you say publish, the change is added to your repository, Cloudflare builds the website from it, and the new version is live within a couple of minutes. Nothing reaches your visitors until you say so.

## What it costs you

### Does GitHub cost anything?

No. GitHub's free plan for organisations includes private repositories and as many members as you need, which is everything your website uses. Your files stay private to the people you allow. The website itself is public, as a website should be.

### Is the hosting really free?

For most sites, yes. Cloudflare serves plain files, meaning your pages, pictures and stylesheet, free and without limit. We build your pages as plain files, so a visit costs nothing, however many people come.

Only code counts: your forms, and anything else that runs a Worker. The free plan allows 100,000 of those a day, more than the forms on most organisations' sites will ever use.

### What if my forms get very busy?

Then Cloudflare's paid plan, from US$5 a month for your whole account, with 10 million requests to your code included each month. Beyond that, you pay a little for what you use: a month with 15 million requests, each taking about 7 milliseconds of processing, would cost about US$8 in all. Cloudflare's pricing page, listed under "Where these figures come from", has the exact rates.

We watch your usage, and tell you when we recommend moving to the paid plan, so the move is your decision.

If a free allowance does run out, nothing is bought for you. Your forms pause until the next day, and your pages carry on, because they are plain files.

### What does my domain cost?

Your domain is registered with Cloudflare at the registry's own price, with no markup. Most cost £10 to £40 a year, depending on the ending. We check the price, and the price to renew it, with you before you buy.

Free hosting doesn't make the address free. It renews every year, and it is yours for as long as you renew it.

### Are these costs in your monthly price?

No, and that is deliberate. Our monthly price pays for changing and looking after your website. Anything GitHub, Cloudflare or your email provider charges is charged to you directly, at their price. We never mark it up, because we never hold it.

## If you leave

### Can I move my website somewhere else?

Yes. You already have everything: the files, the accounts and the domain, with a handover note that another developer or agent can follow. Your pages are plain HTML and can go to any host. Your forms are written for Cloudflare, and would need adapting.

A domain registered with Cloudflare uses Cloudflare to direct its visitors. You can point it at a new host whenever you like and keep it with Cloudflare. To manage it somewhere else entirely, you move the domain to another registrar.

### Can I keep changing my website after I leave?

Yes, two ways. Any developer, or an AI agent you trust, can follow the handover note. Or you can take your own copy of our publishing agent, set up in your own Claude account, and carry on asking for changes in your in-tray as before. That is a one-off price, on [Prices](https://unremarkable.me/prices/#take-your-own-agent).

## Asking a question

### How do I ask something that isn't answered here?

Email [hey@unremarkable.me](mailto:hey@unremarkable.me). A person reads every email. Unremarkable isn't taking work yet, so for now it's for talking about the idea.

## Where these figures come from

Checked against GitHub's and Cloudflare's own pages on 10 November 2026. Prices change, so we check them again before you buy anything.

- [GitHub's plans](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/learning-about-github/githubs-plans)
- [Cloudflare Workers pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/)
- [Cloudflare: billing for plain files](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/)
- [Cloudflare Registrar questions](https://developers.cloudflare.com/registrar/faq/)

## Next

[Start a website](https://unremarkable.me/start/)

# A worked example

Canonical page: https://unremarkable.me/worked-example/

> **Design fiction.** Unremarkable is written as if it were a business. It isn't taking work yet. What that means: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

A real job, start to finish: one folder in, one finished piece out.

This is a worked example. The job is real: Blind Ant's own publishing agent, the one Cloud Dancer is modelled on, did it for blind-ant.com on 5 November 2026, and you can open the result. Nothing on this page publishes anything.

## The request

Charlotte Joanne, who runs blind-ant.com, put one folder in Blind Ant's in-tray. There was no form, no fields and no instructions, just what she already had:

- Two press releases, as Word documents
- One picture, the mark of an invented company

The agent checks the in-tray twice a day.

## The result

A new piece of three pages: the piece itself and the two releases, with headings, lists, links, a described picture, the licence, and a Markdown version of every page for agents. Open it on your own device, the way you would check a change to your own site.

[Red DOG, on blind-ant.com](https://blind-ant.com/pieces/red-dog/)

## What the agent reported

Every job ends with a receipt, written for the owner. This one said:

- **Her words:** unchanged. The two headlines became the page titles, her section headings became headings, her lists became lists, and "A realistic order of work" became a numbered list. The email address in the text became a link.
- **Typos fixed:** none found.
- **Lines the agent wrote itself:** the piece's description, two paragraphs about it, a section on what is invented and what is real, and the picture's alt text and description, each quoted word for word in the receipt so she could check them.
- **Checks:** one main heading on every page, no sideways scrolling on a phone or a desktop, and nothing changed but the new piece.
- **What it couldn't check:** "NOT VERIFIED: I could not fetch the live page." The next morning's run checked that the site had been built and published, and said so.
- **The question:** "Please confirm reddog@blind-ant.com is a mailbox that exists."

## The decision

The receipt ended: "Say 'pull it' to take the Piece down." The owner decides. The agent never has the last word.

Blind Ant runs its agent in live mode, because a design fiction studio can afford to publish first and pull later. Your site starts the other way round: with Cloud Dancer, the same job stops at a private copy of your site, and nothing reaches your visitors until you say so. If you come to trust it, you can choose live mode for the small things.

## What it shows

- You give us what you have, in the form you have it. Nobody copies it into fields.
- Your words stay yours. Anything the agent writes is set out for you to check.
- The agent says what it couldn't do, and asks what it doesn't know, instead of guessing.
- You decide what stays live.

[Start a website](https://unremarkable.me/start/)

# Accessibility statement

Canonical page: https://unremarkable.me/accessibility/

> **Design fiction.** Unremarkable is written as if it were a business. It isn't taking work yet. What that means: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

An accessibility statement is where most sites admit what they couldn't manage. Ours is built to [Zero Information Casualty version 1.7](https://zeroinformationcasualty.org/), so that nobody, whether reading directly, using assistive technology or sending an agent, loses access to anything published here.

New to the subject? [What is web accessibility?](https://unremarkable.me/what-is-accessibility/) explains it, in the words of the W3C Web Accessibility Initiative and our own.

## How it is built

- Every page is plain, static HTML. No content depends on JavaScript, and the site uses none.
- Each page has one main heading, headings in order, landmark regions and a skip link to the main content.
- Text sizes are relative, so the site respects your browser's text size and zoom.
- All text meets WCAG AAA contrast, at least 7:1, in both the light scheme and the dark scheme, which follows your system setting. If your system asks for more contrast, secondary text and dividing lines change to the full text colour. Measured on 8 November 2026: body text 16.2:1 and 16.8:1, secondary text 9.4:1 and 9.9:1, the berry accent 9.0:1 and 9.7:1.
- Nothing moves, so there is nothing to switch off for reduced motion.

## Standards and testing

The site aims to meet WCAG 2.2 at level AA as a baseline, alongside Zero Information Casualty v1.7, and is tested with a screen reader as it changes.

This is a statement of how the site is built and what it aims for, not a claim of certified conformance. No independent audit has been carried out.

This statement was last reviewed on 10 November 2026.

## Found and fixed

- **7 November 2026: numbers read twice.** The list of work was numbered by the stylesheet, so VoiceOver read each number as well as the item's place in the list. It is now a real numbered list, and the numbers you can see are hidden from screen readers.
- **7 November 2026: a link to the page you were on.** On the home page, the name at the top linked to the home page and repeated the heading below it. It was removed.
- **9 November 2026: an email box nobody could fill in.** The fix form showed the owner's address in a read-only email field, straight after saying it doesn't ask who you are. It is now a sentence saying where reports go. Found in a review by another AI, Codex.
- **9 November 2026: one way of reading.** The fix form let you choose only one way of reading the page, though many people use a screen reader with braille, or a magnifier with the keyboard. You can now choose all that apply. Found in the same review.
- **9 November 2026: a link to the page you were on, in the menu.** The current page was a link to itself, so NVDA said "same page link, current page". It is still named as the current page, but is no longer a link. Found by listening to a sister site.
- **9 November 2026: "Design fiction" said twice.** The note under each heading was a landmark named Design fiction that began with those words. It is now a plain note. Found the same way.
- **9 November 2026: columns that could overflow.** With text enlarged on a narrow screen, the "How we build" columns could be wider than the page. They now shrink to fit. Found in the same review.
- **10 November 2026: a comma on its own.** On the home page, NVDA read "Cloud Dancer" and then the comma after it separately, because the comma came straight after the bold name. Phix had the same problem. Both sentences now start with the name and carry straight on. Found by listening to the redesigned home page with NVDA.
- **10 November 2026: a colon after a link.** On the home page, the colon after the link to Zero Information Casualty was read on its own. The sentence now starts with the link. Found the same way.
- **10 November 2026: a picture described in two halves.** On the About page, NVDA split the photo's description across two lines and said "graphic" before each half. The description is now short enough to be read in one go. Found by listening to the page with NVDA, reading through and tabbing.
- **10 November 2026: an address box you didn't need.** The fix form showed the address of the page you came from in a text field, already filled in. On iPhone, VoiceOver stopped on it and spelled out the address, and nobody needed to change it. It is now a sentence saying which page the report is about. You're only asked for an address if we don't know it.

## Reporting a problem

Every page has a link at the foot, "Fix something on this page", to a short form that already knows which page you were on. You can also use it for any site Unremarkable built.

When you send a report, you get a link to its own page. It shows what you sent and where it stands, and once the fix is live it asks whether it works for you. You can answer there, so we never need your email address. Reports are read first by Phix (said "fix"), our fixing agent, built on Claude, and the site's owner decides every fix that goes live. The link ends in a long random key; anyone who has it can see the report, and nobody else can.

The form doesn't ask who you are. We keep what you write, the page's address, how you were reading the page if you tell us, and your browser and device as your browser reports them. We don't keep your name, your email address or your IP address. Reports are used only to fix the sites, and to learn what to get right on the next one. Each report is deleted 12 months after it is sent, and the [privacy page](https://unremarkable.me/privacy/) says how to have yours deleted sooner.

The Start form, for starting a website, keeps nothing while Unremarkable is design fiction: what you write is checked and thrown away.

## For agents

Agents acting for a person are welcome on every public page. There is a summary for agents at [llms.txt](https://unremarkable.me/llms.txt), the full text of the site in one file at [llms-full.txt](https://unremarkable.me/llms-full.txt), and a Markdown version of every page alongside it. All of them are generated from the pages you are reading when the site is built, not maintained by hand.

The site's permissions for search indexing and model training are declared separately in its [robots.txt file](https://unremarkable.me/robots.txt).

# What is web accessibility?

Canonical page: https://unremarkable.me/what-is-accessibility/

> **Design fiction.** Unremarkable is written as if it were a business. It isn't taking work yet. What that means: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

A website should work for the people who come to it. That includes people who read with their eyes, listen with a screen reader, use braille, enlarge the text, or navigate without a mouse.

Accessibility shapes the design, the words and how everything works. The W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI) introduces it like this:

## An introduction from W3C WAI

> When websites and web tools are properly designed and coded, people with disabilities can use them. However, currently many sites and tools are developed with accessibility barriers that make them difficult or impossible for some people to use.
>
> Making the web accessible benefits individuals, businesses, and society. International web standards define what is needed for accessibility.

Reproduced unchanged from [Introduction to Web Accessibility](https://www.w3.org/WAI/fundamentals/accessibility-intro/), W3C Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI). Edited by Shawn Lawton Henry; developed by the Education and Outreach Working Group. Updated 3 February 2026. Copyright © 2026 World Wide Web Consortium.

## What that means at Unremarkable

People come to a website to do something: find an answer, choose a service, book a place. They need to be able to complete that task using the devices and ways of reading that work for them.

We build accessibility into the design and development of a site. Every kind of page is listened to by someone who uses a screen reader every day. We also check things that listening alone cannot establish, including text contrast and how the layout responds when text is enlarged.

Screen reader testing is one part of that work. Accessibility also involves people with hearing, movement, speech, cognitive and other disabilities. One person's experience cannot stand for everyone's.

Our approach brings together WCAG, the international Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, and [Zero Information Casualty](https://zeroinformationcasualty.org/), the standard we build to so that published information reaches people however they read it.

You can read about this site's implementation, testing and fixes in our [accessibility statement](https://unremarkable.me/accessibility/).

## Explore further

These resources come from W3C WAI:

- [Introduction to Web Accessibility](https://www.w3.org/WAI/fundamentals/accessibility-intro/) explains what accessibility means, why it matters and what making a website accessible involves.
- [How People with Disabilities Use the Web](https://www.w3.org/WAI/people-use-web/) explores people's experiences, the barriers they encounter and the tools they use.
- [Accessibility Principles](https://www.w3.org/WAI/fundamentals/accessibility-principles/) introduces the principles behind accessible websites and applications.

The quotation above is third-party material. It is covered by the W3C Software and Document License, separately from Unremarkable's Creative Commons licence. Its reproduction does not imply endorsement by W3C or WAI.

# Privacy

Canonical page: https://unremarkable.me/privacy/

> **Design fiction.** Unremarkable is written as if it were a business. It isn't taking work yet. What that means: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

Only one form on this site keeps anything: "Fix something on this page". This is what it keeps, for how long, and how to have it deleted.

## What is kept

What you write in your report, the address of the page it is about, how you were reading the page if you tell us, and your browser and device as your browser reports them. We don't ask for your name or your email address, and we don't keep your IP address: it is used for a moment to stop the form being flooded, then forgotten.

Your report is read by Phix (said "fix"), our fixing agent, built on Claude, and by the person who looks after the site it is about. Anyone who has your report's link can see it, because the link is the only key, so keep it to yourself.

## How long it is kept

Twelve months from the day you send it. Then the report, and everything that happened to it, is deleted automatically, and its link stops working.

## Having a report deleted sooner

Email [hey@unremarkable.me](mailto:hey@unremarkable.me) with your report's link, and it will be deleted. The link is how we know the report is yours, so you needn't tell us who you are.

## The Start form

The Start form keeps nothing while Unremarkable is design fiction. What you write is checked and thrown away. When that changes, this page will say exactly what it keeps before you send anything.

## Who is responsible

[Charli-Jo Tyrer](https://charli-jo.com/) runs Unremarkable and answers for what this site keeps. Questions go to the same address, [hey@unremarkable.me](mailto:hey@unremarkable.me).


---

# As if

Canonical page: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

> **Design fiction.** Unremarkable is written as if it were a business. It isn't taking work yet. What that means: https://unremarkable.me/as-if/

This site is written as if Unremarkable were a business. It isn't one yet.

Unremarkable is real: it is the name at the foot of every site listed under "Our work" on the home page, and those sites are real. What isn't real yet is the business those pages describe, a studio that designs, builds and looks after websites for organisations. This site works that business out by building it properly before it exists. That is design fiction, and this page is its standard.

## Who runs it

Unremarkable is run by [Charli-Jo Tyrer](https://charli-jo.com/), who answers for everything on this site and everything its agents do.

Want to talk about this idea? Email [hey@unremarkable.me](mailto:hey@unremarkable.me). A person reads every email.

## The As If standard

1. **Inside, everything is done for real.** Prices, terms and the way in are written as the real business would write them, and built to the same standard as everything else Unremarkable makes. Unremarkable never is, even when it is pretending.
2. **Outside, every page says so.** Directly under each page's main heading, in the same words and the same place, a note says this is design fiction and that Unremarkable isn't taking work yet. It is part of the page, never small print, so a screen reader reaches it straight after the heading.
3. **Nobody is misled.** Anything that would take something from you, your name, your email address or your money, tells you first that the business isn't trading, and keeps nothing until it is.
4. **Agents are told too.** The site's llms.txt and the Markdown version of every page carry the same note, so an agent sent to hire Unremarkable reports back accurately.

## What is real here

- The sites listed under "Our work" on the home page, each built to Zero Information Casualty and tested with a screen reader.
- The "Fix something on this page" link on every page. A person reads every report, and fixes go live.
- The accessibility statement, which describes this site as it actually is.
- The [privacy page](https://unremarkable.me/privacy/), which says what the fix form keeps and for how long.
- The email address, [hey@unremarkable.me](mailto:hey@unremarkable.me).
- The worked example: a real job done for blind-ant.com by Blind Ant's publishing agent, the one Cloud Dancer is modelled on, with its receipt.

## What is not real yet

- The prices and the terms. They are worked out with care, but nobody can buy them.
- The "Start" form. It works, checks what you write and shows you what would happen next, but it keeps nothing and sends nothing.
- The in-tray for clients' sites, with a private copy before anything goes live. Blind Ant's publishing already runs from an in-tray on its own, twice a day, in live mode: that is the worked example. The version with a private copy for a client is designed, not built.

## When it becomes real

This page will say so and give the date. The note will come off every page, and the Start form will begin keeping what you send, with a privacy notice that says exactly what, before you send it.
